toc.title: Three benefits for the busy person

sections.title: Find the calmest spot in your home
Know what helps you feel calm

blocks.p: No, you are not too busy to start bringing meditative or mindfulness practices into your daily life. I should know, because I'm busy too. Here are some easy meditation tips for beginners that can help you reduce your stress, so you can be more productive and effective in all areas of your life, not just work.
Traditionally, we know meditation as the practice of training your mind to focus on a single point: a thought, maybe your breath, a mantra, or a specific visualization.

I think it can be practical and accessible for anybody, even busy people who would rather spend their time doing something else, being more productive. Do you need a 30-day silent retreat? No, I don't think so. Do you need to meditate for 30 minutes a day? I don't think so either. So do me a favor: set aside your assumptions, and I promise I can make this approachable for anyone.

A busy person is someone who doesn't slow down. They're always doing something: taking the kids to school or to practices, maybe running a business, socializing, cleaning, and more. This person feels stressed and overwhelmed pretty much all the time.

On top of that, this person may not be considering that they need to slow down. They think spending time being mindful is ridiculous when they have so much more to do. If this describes you, you're in the right place. And trust me, I can relate. I'll share more about myself toward the end. I won't judge you if you don't judge me. Deal?

blocks.h: Three benefits for the busy person

blocks.p: Busy people prioritize their busyness, thinking that slowing down will only hinder their productivity. But meditation has numerous potential benefits, even for the busy person. Here are three.

One of meditation's most commonly cited benefits is its ability to reduce stress and anxiety. When we experience stress, our body releases cortisol, a hormone that can negatively affect our health. Meditation has been shown to lower cortisol levels, leading to improved mood and decreased anxiety. The National Institutes of Health says mindfulness meditation lowers the cortisol levels in the blood, suggesting that it can lower stress and may decrease the risk of diseases that arise from stress, such as psychiatric disorder, peptic ulcer, and migraine.

By training your mind to focus on a single point, such as your breath or a visualization, you can learn to block out distractions and stay focused on your experience of the present moment. That can be particularly beneficial for people juggling multiple daily responsibilities and tasks.

Meditation can help you think more clearly, with less mental clutter. It can also reduce emotional dysregulation. Combine those two, and the result could be more goal-directed activity and more productivity. Indeed, as the National Institutes of Health says, meditation may be associated with structural changes in the areas of the brain that are important for sensory, cognitive, and emotional processing, and the data further suggest that meditation may impact age-related declines in cortical structure.

Put simply, meditation is good for your brain and good for productivity. Being more productive frees up some time for less busyness. And having more emotional regulation means the things that typically stress you out won't be as stress-inducing.

blocks.why: This article talks about mindfulness. This practice gives you a few minutes of it.

blocks.p: You may be thinking meditation is just woo-woo stuff. But meditation and mindfulness don't only improve general connection and awareness of the present moment. There are more concrete potential benefits as well.

I personally have no interest in woo-woo. I need evidence. I like data, maybe just like you. I need things to make sense, and I need to see the benefit. Numerous studies have shown improvements in a range of behavioral problems, or reductions in the intensity of symptoms, through mindfulness-based interventions: blood pressure, insomnia and sleep, anxiety and depression, and even cancer. Not the cancer itself, but the psychological distress of someone going through cancer treatment. Also fatigue and sleep disturbance, pain, and symptoms of anxiety and depression.

As a busy person, you may assume meditation has no place in your life. I don't need you to be a meditation guru. I don't need you to be a yogi. I don't need you up on a mountaintop. I think it can be simple and accessible to anyone, regardless of background or experience. I actually think meditation is an ideal practice for busy people who don't have much time to spare, because even a few minutes a day can make a big difference.

ol: Allow positive emotions. Meditation doesn't need to be empty-minded, and I don't need you to summon negative experiences. Instead, purposefully call up more positive emotions through your memory. For example, when I remember the birth of my children, and how they grabbed my finger with their tiny newborn hands, I feel happiness and connection. I can mindfully allow those emotions to be in the present moment.

Focus on your breath. This is one of the simplest and most popular meditation techniques. Close your eyes if you'd like, and focus on your breath, inhaling and exhaling deeply and slowly. When your mind wanders, gently bring your attention back to your breath. That said, I don't like to recommend prescribed breathing. I like to say: let your body breathe how it naturally knows how to, and how it naturally needs to. It will take care of you. So another option is to let that be, and focus on your body's natural breathing.

Scan your body. Focus on each part of your body, from the top of your head to your toes. Notice any sensations you feel, without judgment, as best you can. Allow a range of emotions to make themselves present, both negative and positive. It's just checking in with yourself from top to bottom and seeing what you see.

Visualize. Imagine a peaceful place or situation, such as a beach or a quiet forest. Let yourself fully immerse in the visualization, and hopefully release any stress or anxiety. I often ask my therapy clients where they would go to feel safe. Focus on the details of the scene you create in your mind, and what it would be like to experience that environment directly through your senses. Even though you're imagining it, you can still imagine what your senses might pick up there.

Use guided practices. If you struggle with meditation, find a guided practice. There are lots out there for free, or you can use an app like Calm. I like that one. Pick and choose what works best for you and dump the rest, in my opinion. I prefer something really concrete and very directive. If it involves beams of light entering me, I'll pass.

blocks.p: You're a busy person, so your meditation opportunities might come less often than would be ideal. Prepare ahead of time so you get the most out of your time and out of the practice.

blocks.h3: Find the calmest spot in your home

blocks.p: Pick the spot in your home that is the most calming for you. A calming environment provides passive safety cues. These are things that tell your body, your system, that you are safe and that it can calm down. You can also alter the environment to increase those cues, enhancing them through minor adjustments:

ul: Use a soothing scent to help you slow down.
Dim the lighting, or let in natural light.

blocks.h3: Know what helps you feel calm

blocks.p: Before trying to meditate, know what helps you feel safe and calm. Knowing ahead of time streamlines your efforts by eliminating the guesswork. Some things to consider:

ul: What scent is the most efficient at bringing you a sense of calm?
What time of day is ideal?
What sounds do you prefer, or is quiet better for you?

blocks.p: If you don't know, that's okay. You can experiment with something different each time, prune out what doesn't work for you, and build on what does. I personally tend to prefer silence, or maybe some lo-fi chill hop music.

If you're like me, there is a nearly 100% chance you'll be interrupted or distracted during meditation: kids, spouse, chores, and thoughts that keep popping up about other things that need to be done. So deal with distractions ahead of time if you can. Think about what will likely happen. A few tips:

ul: Meditate when everyone's asleep, either early in the morning or at night.
Turn off your phone and every other device you need to.
Put on the right kind of music to help you focus inward, if you need it.
Tell anyone and everyone you need to that you need five minutes to be alone.

blocks.p: I told you I won't judge you if you don't judge me, so I'll confide in you: I am one of those busy people.

My wife and I are very active parents. As a dad, I pack lunches, I drop the kids off and pick them up from school, I do the after-school practices, and I play with my kids every day. I'm an active spouse. My wife and I are partners in everything, and we prize our time together, even if we're just watching Netflix. I'm a homeowner, with chores and more chores, including a pain-in-the-butt pool that needs constant attention. I hate cooking, so I clean the dishes afterward. That's my part.

I also work full time as a therapist, and I have a private practice on Saturday mornings and some weeknights. I'm a content creator, with the blog, this podcast, and my YouTube channel. I'm a course creator and a book writer, and a whole bunch of other business things eat up my time. That's just a broad overview. If you looked at the minute-to-minute of my day, you'd see me being productive pretty much constantly.

But in my opinion, busy is not necessarily bad. Are you worried about me yet? Don't be. I love it. The stuff I do doesn't feel like work. I genuinely enjoy what I do for a living and what I create. I love being a dad, I love being a husband, and I think my wife and I are doing a pretty damn good job raising our kiddos. My health is good, and from what I hear from people, I'm making a significant impact. So what looks like busy on the outside is busy, yes. But it's also my passion and my fulfillment.

Do I feel stress sometimes? Sure, and that's when I know I need to slow down. Ideally, I slow myself down and do some mindfulness and meditation before the stress comes on. Stress is not bad. It can be quite motivating, honestly. But I balance it out with quality time with my family and moments of peace during the day. I do lots and lots of check-ins with myself throughout the day. And yes, I'll sit down and meditate for 20 minutes when I need to. More often than not, it's about five minutes.

If you're busy like me, find time for short bursts of meditation. Be honest with yourself. Slow down before there's a problem. Take in the present moment with a breath, and listen to your body. Trust me, it is worth it.
Before you get down to work, spend five minutes with your internal experience, as best you can. It will ultimately make you more productive, more focused, and less stressed.
